entities.name: Theuderic III
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Theuderic III (c. 657–691 CE) was a Merovingian King of the Franks who nominally reigned over Neustria and Burgundy from 673 to 675, and then continuously from 679 until his death in 691, also controlling Austrasia from 679. His reign, largely defined by the increasing power of the Mayors of the Palace, particularly Pippin II of Herstal, marks a crucial phase in the decline of Merovingian royal authority and the ascendance of the Carolingian dynasty. He served as a symbolic figurehead during a period of intense internal Frankish power struggles, embodying the "roi fainéant" archetype.

Following the death of Childeric II, Theuderic III was briefly placed on the throne of Neustria and Burgundy in 673 by Ebroin, the powerful Mayor of the Palace. His initial reign was cut short by a rebellion that saw him tonsured and exiled to the Abbey of Saint-Denis. Recalled in 679 after a period of instability and civil war, he was reinstated as king, and following the Battle of Tertry in 687, his authority, though symbolic, was extended over Austrasia, effectively uniting the Frankish realms under the de facto control of Pippin II. This victory solidified Pippin's position as the sole Mayor of the Palace, eclipsing the Merovingian monarch entirely.

Theuderic III's reign thus represents a pivotal moment in the transition of power from the Merovingian kings to the Carolingian Mayors of the Palace. His long tenure, despite his limited personal influence, provided a facade of royal legitimacy for Pippin II's consolidation of power across the Frankish kingdoms. The institutionalization of the "do-nothing king" model under Theuderic laid the groundwork for the eventual deposition of the Merovingians by Pippin the Short a few decades later, fundamentally reshaping the political landscape of early medieval Western Europe.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Theuderic III's reign, though personally inconsequential, was critical in the structural shift of power from the Merovingian monarchy to the Carolingian Mayors of the Palace, directly enabling Pippin II's consolidation of Frankish authority. This systemic change laid the foundation for the Carolingian Empire.
